items.why: The negation applies to changing his ways, while appointing priests is affirmed.
Distinguishes the buried man’s earlier prophecy from the speaker’s assurance to his sons.
Distinguishes the collective defeat of four descendants from Jonathan’s killing of one.
The final “him” refers to the officer addressed as “you,” not the man of God.
Tracks the old prophet as rider while his sons only saddle the donkey.
The two covenants overlap in participants, but only the first includes the Lord.
Separates the closing succession event from the earlier aside about recording Uzziah’s reign.
Distinguishes the stated cause of Uzziah’s eagerness from the priests’ preceding action.
Orders the proposed ambush correctly, though the Arameans’ intention is only the king’s claim.
Distinguishes rejected hypothetical destinations from the men’s actual decision to surrender.
Requires ordering two similar battles at Gob and retaining the killer associated with each.
“The news” is a generic repeated label, and the camp is a weak competing reporting object.
Resolves “Seize him” to the man confronting the king rather than the king issuing the order.
Separates the priests who follow from Uzziah, the antecedent of “him.”
Tracks “my son” to the quoted other woman and assigns his planned consumption to tomorrow.
Attaches “who instructed him” to Zechariah rather than the previously mentioned father.
Distinguishes Elisha’s response to the officer from his earlier announcement of food prices.
Distinguishes the binding divine command from the hypothetical offer of possessions.
The talking continues after eating and immediately precedes Paul’s departure.
Requires only ordering three coordinated actions: mobilizing, marching, and laying siege.
Separates Jehoiada, the giver, from David, the weapons’ former owner inside a relative clause.
Keeps the accusers ordered to present a case distinct from the earlier tribunal.
The purpose is making Uzziah king; the competing answer supplies background cause instead.
Resolves “their command” to the family leaders rather than the officials who mustered the army.
Tracks the departing man of God despite the intervening prophet becoming the grammatical subject.
Tracks the trampled “him” to the appointed officer rather than the king who appointed him.
The instruction “are all to guard the temple” includes both on-duty and off-duty companies.
Requires distinguishing sender and addressee roles in the brief letter heading.
Identifies the slain Philistine as Ishbi-Benob while keeping David in the rescued role.
Distinguishes the corrective plan after their admission from their earlier concealment of valuables.
Tracks the young man as the information bearer within Paul’s instruction and the centurion’s report.
Distinguishes the immediately preceding report from the messengers’ earlier pursuit.
Resolves the causal “he loved the soil” to Uzziah rather than his workers.
Maps “my son” to the woman addressing the king and distinguishes him from the hidden child.
Separates the king requesting prayer from the man of God who performs it.
Separates peoples God helped Uzziah fight from the Ammonites who brought tribute.
Uses the narrated city-then-tomb sequence rather than selecting the final burial location.
Resolves the hidden child through Joash’s family relationships; Ahaziah has already died.
Separates the explicit cause of calm from the people’s accompanying rejoicing.
Distinguishes the centurions receiving the order from the soldiers they must prepare.
Separates the supposed hirer, Israel’s king, from the kings supposedly hired to attack.
Identifies the murderer as the sender of the executioner, not the messenger being sent.
Tracks “him” and “he” to the man of God within the old prophet’s quoted claim.
The explicit “because” clause supplies the answer; the lamps offer no credible competing cause.
Tracks the returning soldiers against the cavalry continuing with Paul across contrasting clauses.
Tracks the beaten “they” to Sceva’s sons while the possessed man remains the attacker.
Cured illnesses can also be described as leaving, so the competing answer is not clearly excluded.
Identifies the commander as the requested transporter within the conspirators’ instructions to the council.
Orders gathering, burning, and valuation rather than jumping to the later calculation.
The explicit sword command targets her followers, although the woman is also subsequently executed.
Distinguishes the noise prompting Athaliah’s movement from what she sees after arriving.
Distinguishes the consent the ambushers await from the council appearance used as their pretext.
Separates the prophet receiving the revelation from the man of God addressed by its warning.
Tracks the future oracle’s acting subject to Josiah rather than Jeroboam in the surrounding scene.
